analysis.one_liner: Phases out government-guaranteed private student lending and lends directly to students, with income-based repayment plans.
analysis.headline: A Senate committee held a hearing on this direct student lending bill in May 1993 but never voted it out of committee; its core proposal became law later that year through a separate budget bill.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced the Federal Family Education Loan program — where private banks lend to students and the federal government guarantees the loans, paying the banks subsidies and insurance — with a program where the federal government lends to students directly, phased in over four school years. It would have offered borrowers a choice of repayment plans, including one that ties monthly payments to income, so that loan bills would not push people away from lower-paying public-service careers. It also set interest-rate ceilings on the new direct loans and directed a study of how Sallie Mae, the government-sponsored loan reseller, would fit into the new system.
analysis.who_benefits: Student and parent borrowers, who would deal with one federal lender instead of a chain of banks, guaranty agencies, and servicers; taxpayers, since the government would stop paying banks to do lending it could do itself; and graduates who want lower starting pay in community service, teaching, or government work, who would have an income-based repayment option instead of a fixed bill they cannot afford.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the guaranteed private-lender loan system with a Federal Direct Student Loan Program, phased in so direct loans reach 4% of new loan volume in the first year, 25% the second, 60% the third, and 100% by the fourth.
States its purpose as avoiding 'the unnecessary cost, to taxpayers and borrowers, and administrative complexity' of the guaranteed loan program.

Offers four repayment plans, including an income-contingent 'EXCEL account' whose payments are based on the borrower's income, so repayment obligations 'do not foreclose community service-oriented career choices.'
Caps interest rates on the new direct loans (9% for Stafford loans, 10% for parent PLUS loans, 11% for supplemental student loans) and sets Treasury-bill-based rates after 1997.
Adds deferments for up to three years of unemployment or economic hardship, forbearance during national service, and the right to consolidate loans into one direct loan.

analysis.who_pays: Private banks, guaranty agencies, and Sallie Mae would lose the guaranteed federal business the current system gives them: the bill terminates a guaranty-agency administrative allowance, declares guaranty-agency reserve funds federal property, and directs a study of Sallie Mae's transition out of its government-sponsored status. Borrowers would pay a loan fee of 5% to 6.5% of principal and would lose the ability to wipe out these loans in bankruptcy, and would forgo financial privacy to the extent the IRS was used to collect income-based payments.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes direct loans nondischargeable in bankruptcy and charges borrowers a loan fee of not less than 5% of principal, so it tightens borrower obligations even as it simplifies lending.

To run income-based repayment, the IRS would disclose borrowers' tax return information — identity, filing status, and adjusted gross income — to the Department of Education, and the bill plans possible IRS wage-withholding collection of loans.

It concentrates power in the Education Secretary: guaranty agencies can have their agreements terminated and functions assumed, may not file for bankruptcy in that case, state courts are barred from interfering, and no institution has any right to participate in the direct loan program.
As a backstop, if budget sequestration forces cuts to the direct loan program, the bill's answer is to raise the loan fee charged to borrowers by 0.5%.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers and taxpayers the trade is heavily favorable: a simpler loan delivered by one federal lender, an income-based payment option that protects graduates taking lower-paying public-service jobs, and the end of subsidies paid to private middlemen for lending the government could do itself. The real costs fall on the guaranteed-loan industry, which loses its federally guaranteed franchise, and on borrowers in two specific ways — these loans can never be discharged in bankruptcy and a 5-6.5% fee comes off the top. The privacy and power concerns around IRS involvement and the Secretary's authority over guaranty agencies are legitimate but standard for any federal collection system; the bill's phase-in and transition funding for guaranty agencies show the drafters took the disruption seriously.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which held one hearing but never voted to send it to the floor, and the Congress ended with the bill still sitting in committee.

narrative.text: Introduced on May 6, 1993 by Sen. Kennedy with five other senators listed as original sponsors, and read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
The committee held hearings on the bill on May 26, 1993, printed as S.Hrg. 103-188.
No further action was ever taken; no committee vote, no floor vote, and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 with the bill still in committee.

The core of the proposal did not stay dead: later in 1993 Congress enacted direct student lending as part of the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act, phasing in the federal direct loan program much as this bill envisioned.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: On this bill's own record, the guaranteed student loan industry — the banks, guaranty agencies, and Sallie Mae that the bill would have phased out — kept its guaranteed federal business because the bill never reached a vote. In practice, though, students and taxpayers largely got the substance anyway: the direct lending program passed later in 1993 through a budget bill that could not be filibustered, and it ran alongside — not instead of — the guaranteed loan program for years.

sides.party_line_note: Eight senators cosponsored — seven Democrats and one Republican (Durenberger of Minnesota) — and no floor vote ever occurred, so no party-line record exists; the dividing line was between the direct-lending plan and the guaranteed-loan industry, not between parties.

industries.note: The bill phases the guaranteed loan program out entirely over four years, ending the federal guarantees, interest subsidies, and administrative allowances banks earn for lending money the government could lend itself. Under the current system their income comes from a federal guarantee on loans students must repay regardless.

The bill terminates their administrative cost allowance, declares their reserve funds federal property, and lets the Education Secretary terminate their agreements and take over their functions during the transition. Their fees and insurance payouts come from the guaranteed-loan system the bill dismantles.

Its government-sponsored middleman role shrinks as guaranteed lending phases out; the bill requires it to serve as lender-of-last-resort during the transition and directs a study of converting it to an ordinary private corporation. Its business is built on volume in the guaranteed-loan pipeline the bill replaces.

They lose their role serving guaranteed-loan portfolios, but the bill authorizes the Education Secretary to contract out servicing and collection of the new direct loans, so the work continues as federal contracts. Borrowers get one accountable servicer instead of a chain of intermediaries.

Participating institutions get paid origination fees (capped at about $10 per borrower in the first year) and a single direct pipeline for loan funds, with a ban on charging students any fees for loan origination. No institution, however, has a right to participate.
